issues.legal_issue: An appeal abates in its entirety when proceeding without the deceased respondent’s legal representatives could produce a decree contradictory to the decree that became final in that respondent’s favour.
material_facts: The trial court declared the plaintiffs and the deceased respondent to be co-owners entitled to joint possession, although their respective shares were specified.
The deceased respondent was a beneficiary of the trial court decree and had a vested right under it; the property had not been partitioned.
The appellants appealed the decree, but did not bring the deceased respondent’s legal representatives on record within the prescribed time.

The application to condone the delay in seeking substitution was rejected, and the appellate court found that allowing the appeal could result in a decree inconsistent with the decree in favour of the deceased respondent.
issues.conclusion: The appeal abated in its entirety, not merely as to the deceased respondent’s share.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order XXII Rules 4(3) and 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appeal abates against a deceased respondent if legal representatives are not brought on record within the time allowed by law. Whether that abatement extends to the whole appeal depends on the circumstances, particularly whether deciding the appeal against the remaining parties could produce contradictory or inconsistent decrees concerning the same subject matter. The tests stated in State of Punjab v. Nathu Ram, Sri Chand v. M/s Jagdish Pershad Kishan Chand, Ramagya Prasad Gupta v. Brahmadeo Prasad Gupta, Sardar Amarjit Singh Kalra v. Pramod Gupta, and Shahazada Bi v. Halimabi include whether a successful appeal could conflict with the decree that became final against the deceased, whether effective relief remains possible, and whether the decree is joint and inseverable. A co-owner has a right to possession and enjoyment of every part of unpartitioned property jointly with the other co-owners; a stated share does not by itself make the decree severable. The relevant test is whether the decree concerning the remaining parties would be contradictory or inconsistent with the decree that became final for the deceased party.

rule.if: appeal_from_civil_decree and deceased_respondent_benefited_from_decree and deceased_respondent_not_substituted_in_time and (unpartitioned_property_held_in_joint_possession or appeal_success_could_conflict_with_final_decree)

predicates.appeal_from_civil_decree: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a civil court decree.
predicates.deceased_respondent_benefited_from_decre: The deceased respondent held a right under the decree being appealed.
predicates.deceased_respondent_not_substituted_in_t: The appellant did not bring the deceased respondent’s legal representatives on record within the time allowed.
predicates.unpartitioned_property_held_in_joint_pos: The decree concerns unpartitioned property in which the parties were declared co-owners entitled to joint possession.
predicates.appeal_success_could_conflict_with_final: Allowing the appeal against the remaining parties could produce a decree inconsistent with the decree that became final in favour of the deceased respondent.

issues.definition: When an appeal from a civil decree proceeds without timely substitution of a deceased decree-beneficiary, it abates entirely if the joint-property circumstances or the possible outcome make a contradictory decree possible.

issues.legal_issue: The exemption from substitution for a deceased defendant who did not contest the suit is unavailable unless an application for that exemption is presented before judgment is pronounced and is allowed.
material_facts: The deceased defendant did not appear or contest the suit and did not contest the appeal.
No application seeking exemption from substitution was presented before the trial court pronounced judgment.
The exemption was raised after the decree, when the deceased defendant’s legal representatives were not substituted in the appeal.
issues.conclusion: The exemption under Order XXII Rule 4(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure did not apply.
issues.legal_principle: Order XXII Rule 4(4) permits a court, on an application presented before it pronounces judgment, to exempt a plaintiff from the requirement to substitute the legal representatives of a deceased defendant who did not contest the suit or file a written statement. Once the application is allowed, the decree may be treated as having the same force and effect as if pronounced before the defendant’s death. The Court relied on Zahirul Islam v. Mohd. Usman and T. Gnanavel v. T.S. Kanagaraj in holding that the required application must be presented before judgment.

predicates.civil_proceeding_involving_deceased_defe: The proceeding involves a defendant who died before the court pronounced judgment.
predicates.deceased_defendant_did_not_contest: The defendant did not appear to contest the proceeding or file a response contesting it.
predicates.exemption_application_not_presented_befo: No application seeking exemption from substitution was presented to the court before it pronounced judgment.

issues.definition: In a proceeding involving a deceased defendant who did not contest, the exemption from substitution is unavailable if the exemption application was not presented before judgment.
